name: FunctionalPlus (fplus::keep_if)
workload: README example: keep the odd numbers of 5000 random integers, 20000 consecutive runs accumulated, comparing a hand-written loop, std::copy_if and fplus::keep_if.
claimed_speedup: No speedup claimed; parity: hand-written for loop 0.632 s, std::copy_if 0.641 s, fplus::keep_if 0.627 s (fplus::keep_if about 2% below std::copy_if, derived from page data). README: 'the compiler seems to do a very good job optimizing and inlining everything to basically equal machine code performance-wise.'
hardware: 'a standard desktop PC' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only functional-programming helpers (map, filter, fold, compose) over ordinary STL containers; requires C++14. Chained calls can reuse storage when given r-value containers, but not in every case, so complex functions can allocate and copy more than hand-written code. The README contrasts it with range-v3, whose lazy ranges allocate no intermediate containers, but gives no numbers for that.
caveats: This is a parity result, not a speed win: the only number in the README is a single 5000-element keep-odd micro-example in which fplus::keep_if is within about 2% of std::copy_if and a hand loop, and the README itself says the more complex functions could be written more efficiently. Hardware is 'a standard desktop PC', GCC version unstated, and the benchmark source is not linked from the README (no benchmark directory in the repo listing), so it is not reproducible from public code. Single-run style accumulated timing with no spread. The seed list tagged the licence MIT and a filesystems-and-io category; the repo is Boost Software License 1.0 and the library is a general container-algorithm helper, so the category was moved to stdlib-replacements/utilities. Kept as a documented 'not faster' entry.

name: G3log
baseline: std::fstream with std::flush after every line (also Boost.Log); not faster than stdio fprintf+fflush in the same table
workload: Third-party (reckless) benchmark: average latency of one log call from a single thread while 64 GiB of raw data is written to 2048 files in parallel (2048 log entries), every library flushing to the OS per call; plus Mandelbrot total-overhead rows with 4 and 8 worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Disk I/O scenario, average call latency relative to reckless = 1.00: g3log 30.71 vs fstream 5719.93, about 186x lower (derived from page data); g3log 30.71 vs boost_log 46.03, about 1.5x lower (derived from page data); g3log is higher than stdio at 17.01 and spdlog at 23.82. Mandelbrot overhead relative to reckless: 4 worker threads g3log 10.58 vs stdio 15.03, fstream 15.66, boost_log 13.17; 8 threads g3log 3.09 vs stdio 3.70, fstream 4.62 (boost_log 1.82 and spdlog 1.87 are lower). First-party README: 'average call ... about ~2 us' on a 2010 laptop, no baseline named.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0; benchmark programs built -O3 -std=c++11 by the reckless Tuprules.lua; g3log 1.3.2 library build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 2700X 3.7 GHz, 8 cores, SMT off, 32 GiB RAM, Samsung 970 EVO SSD, Linux 4.14.65
tradeoffs: Asynchronous logger: log calls format the message at the call site and push it to a queue serviced by a background sink thread, with dynamic sinks and crash-safe flush on fatal signals. Messages queued at a crash are written by the signal handler; throughput is bounded by the single background thread. Unlicense/public domain gives no patent grant.
caveats: The only win is against synchronous baselines under a heavy disk-write load: the 186x figure is mostly std::fstream with std::flush blocking behind a 64 GiB write storm, and g3log is slower than plain stdio fprintf+fflush in that same table. Across the other scenarios in the same document g3log is slow: periodic calls 78.19 vs stdio 43.77, fstream 41.32, spdlog 40.85, boost_log 67.42 (g3log is the slowest library listed), call burst 4.20 vs stdio 2.55, fstream 2.36, boost_log 3.84, Mandelbrot single thread 13.40 vs stdio 12.21, fstream 10.73. The benchmark is written by the author of a competing library (reckless) with assumptions that favour reckless; the g3log wrapper benchmarks/g3log.hpp that the Tupfile needs is not in the repo (404 at HEAD), so the g3log rows cannot be reproduced from public code. g3log 1.3.2 and gcc 7.3.0 are old. The author's own worst-case-latency comparison (kjellkod.wordpress.com blog linked from the README) could not be reached (host not resolvable), and the README's ~2 us figure is first-party on 2010 hardware with no baseline. A Quill benchmark seen only as a search snippet reportedly lists g3log slowest at tail percentiles (not opened). The repo has test_performance/ (main_threaded_mean.cpp, main_threaded_worst.cpp comparing g3log with Google glog) but no stored results.

name: glog
baseline: Boost.Log 1.56 (trivial severity logger, text file sink)
workload: Wall time to write 1,000,000 log lines to files in a logs directory, from a single thread and from 10 threads sharing one logger; glog uses LOG(INFO) << 'glog message # ' << i with FLAGS_logtostderr=0.
claimed_speedup: spdlog v0.x README table: Boost.Log v1.56 4.207s single thread / 6.592s 10 threads vs glog v0.3.3 1.077s / 1.678s, about 3.9x faster for glog in both cases (derived from page data); spdlog itself 0.975s / 0.961s, i.e. glog is slightly slower than spdlog.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (version not stated) with -march=native -O3 -flto -std=c++11 -pthread, from bench/Makefile at the same spdlog commit (bench/glog-bench.cpp, glog-bench-mt.cpp, boost-bench.cpp, boost-bench-mt.cpp)
tradeoffs: Synchronous logging behind a global mutex: threads serialise, so 10 threads were slower than one in the table (1.678s vs 1.077s). Buffered file output (default flush interval and level) means lines can be lost on a crash unless FLAGS_logbuflevel is changed; global flags and singleton state; no asynchronous mode; the repository is archived and read-only.
caveats: Measured by the maintainer of a competing library (spdlog) in 2014 on glog v0.3.3 and Boost.Log 1.56, both long superseded, and the table is no longer in the current spdlog README. Compiler version and the build flags of the prebuilt libglog (-lglog) and of Boost.Log (built from a personal path in the Makefile) are not stated; the Makefile flags apply only to the benchmark programs. The two sides are not configured identically (glog default buffering and its own file naming, Boost.Log with auto_flush=false and a 10 MiB rotating sink), and the time includes process start-up and log-directory file creation. The seed list gave no performance claim for glog; this is the only numeric comparison found where glog beats a named logger. The RafaGago/logger-bench page (opened) lists glog among its compared libraries but states no results.
